definition: an Amsterdam city permit letting a named venue operate around the clock
The Massachusetts fire code, which sets crowd manager rules for nightclubs, dance halls, discotheques and bars.
The single UK offence created by the Crime and Policing Act (Royal Assent April 29, 2026) that covers spiking, replacing parts of the Offences against the Person Act 1861.
A license to sell beer, wine and spirits, as opposed to a wine and malt (beer and wine) license.
A Boston license, issued by MOCAL Entertainment Licensing, for live acts and DJs or for non-live entertainment such as TVs and background music.
Single-issue prohibition lobbying group founded in Oberlin, Ohio, in 1893; it drove the Eighteenth Amendment.
A code phrase a person can say to venue staff to get discreet help; created in Lincolnshire, England, in 2016.

A building or room classified for groups gathering, such as a club, bar or theater, and held to stricter fire rules than an office or shop. Nightclubs were reclassified this way after the Cocoanut Grove fire.
The eclectic DJ style developed in 1980s Ibiza by DJs including Alfredo Fiorito.
A competitive performance culture built mainly by Black and Latino LGBTQ+ people in New York, organized into houses.
A shared list of barred patrons checked by networked ID scanners, as in Queensland.
A bar-sales target an organizer commits to in place of a rental fee; the organizer pays any shortfall.
Bar assistant who restocks ice, glassware and bottles and clears for bartenders.
Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, the Belleville, Michigan, schoolfriends credited with creating techno.
A project's estimated benefits divided by its costs; the Night Tube case estimated about 2.7 to 1.
The 1990s link between Detroit techno artists and Berlin clubs, starting with Underground Resistance at Tresor in 1991.

aka: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research
definition: the New South Wales statistics bureau that measured the effects of Sydney's lockout laws
A reserved table that comes with bottles bought at a set, high price, usually against a minimum spend.
Training venue staff to notice and step in when someone may be at risk; the Massachusetts DPH's preferred measure over test kits (2024).
NYPD permit required of nightclub musicians and workers from 1940 to 1967.
New York City's 1926 rule requiring a license for music, singing or dancing where food or drink was sold; repealed in 2017.
A small sticker staff put over your phone's camera lenses at the door so photos and video cannot be taken inside.
The permit saying a building may be used for a given purpose; Happy Land had none.
the hour after which a licensed venue may no longer sell or serve alcohol; in US statutes usually written as a window when sales are banned, such as 2 a.m. to 8 a.m.
A recurring party run by a promoter that rents or moves between venues rather than owning a permanent bar.
Berlin's association of club operators and promoters.
Boston's official adult entertainment district on lower Washington Street, approved by the Zoning Commission on Nov. 14, 1974.
A Massachusetts license to serve food to the public; most Boston entertainment license applicants already hold one.
A complimentary ticket, or anything a venue or promoter gives away free, such as entry or a drink.
Rhode Island's post-Station law: ended grandfathering, required sprinklers by occupancy, low-level exit signs and a near-ban on indoor pyrotechnics.
A court-approved settlement requiring a business to change its practices.
A narrower measure covering only food, drink and entertainment businesses, used by Australia's capital-city mayors.
The entry fee charged at the door of a bar or club.
Injury or death from people being compressed in a dense crowd, often with no one running; the cause of death at E2 and in Itaewon.
A trained staff member who keeps exits clear, keeps the count under the limit and leads an orderly exit. Massachusetts requires one for venues of 100 or more, plus one per 250 above 250.
UK government's £1.57 billion pandemic support package for arts, culture and heritage, announced July 2020.
US nonprofit (founded 1998, per Wikipedia) that runs harm reduction booths with drug checking at events in the US and Canada.
A restaurant-industry term for a block of the day, such as breakfast or late night, tracked and marketed separately.
when restricting hours in one area pushes drinkers and problems to neighboring areas, as measured around Sydney's lockout zone
The set of rules, written or not, a venue uses to decide who gets in: ID, sobriety, capacity, dress, group size, guest lists and sometimes crowd fit.
An agreed division of door money between the venue and a promoter or artist, for example 70/30.
UK term for licensed door security staff; the SIA licence fee was £190 as of 2023.
US law making a business liable for harm caused by patrons it served while intoxicated or underage; 43 states and DC have one.
A cap or lid for a glass meant to guard against drink spiking; Boston's nightlife office gave 33,000 to 40 bars and clubs in 2024.
Testing a drug sample and giving the person the result and health information.
The venue deducts set costs from door money before splitting the rest.
A test result that says a substance is absent when it was present; short half-life drugs and partial-structure test kits can both cause them.
The daily pre-opening checklist a Massachusetts crowd manager completes, kept on site for a year.
A promoter pays a set fee to rent the room and keeps the door.
New York term for app-based ride-hail and other car services that are not yellow or green taxis.
An unlicensed, usually outdoor rave with no entry fee, such as Castlemorton Common in May 1992.
A lab method used in drug checking; some chemists and medics have questioned its suitability for the job.
Japan's postwar entertainment-business law, which treated dance clubs as adult entertainment with a curfew until a 2016 amendment
A bar serving an LGBTQ+ crowd; historically one of the first semi-public spaces for queer community in the US.
A drug often linked to spiking; it leaves the body quickly, which can produce false-negative tests. Moved to Class B in the UK in April 2022.
a plastic cup for carrying a drink out of a New Orleans bar onto the street
A UK campaign that the Home Office lists among the anti-spiking schemes it funds.
Letting existing buildings keep operating under the older code rules they were built to. NIST recommended ending it for nightclubs after The Station.
The value an industry adds to the economy, roughly what it sells minus what it buys to make it.
A fixed fee paid to an artist or promoter regardless of turnout.
The artist gets a fixed fee or a share of the door, whichever is greater.
Pre-registered names given reduced or free entry, usually before a cut-off time; not a guarantee of entry.
A promoter paid per person they bring through the door.
The 1984 Massachusetts rule barring free or discounted drinks, unlimited-drink specials, jumbo drinks at regular price and pitchers for fewer than two people.
Policies aimed at reducing harm from drug use rather than only stopping use.
The main billed DJ or act, usually placed at the peak of the night; openers are expected not to play the headliner's music.
A city's request asking the state Legislature to pass a law that applies only to that city; Boston uses it to seek more licenses or later hours.
A chosen-family group in ballroom, led by a mother or father, that competes together at balls.
Dance music named for, and traced to, Chicago's Warehouse club, 1977-1982.
A device that reads the barcode on an ID to check age and authenticity, and can capture name, address and date of birth.
Extra spending and jobs created as nightlife wages and purchases ripple through the rest of the economy.
A promotion giving women free or cheaper entry; unlawful in California since Koire (1985), upheld in some other states.
the final chance to order before service legally ends, usually a few minutes before closing time
The cutoff time for serving alcohol, which can come before the venue closes.
The MBTA's 2014-2016 pilot of weekend subway and bus service until about 2:30 a.m., ended by a 4-0 board vote in 2016.
a Chicago license that extends service from the standard 2 a.m. to 4 a.m. (5 a.m. Sunday), with neighbor notice and sometimes a voter petition
a Texas permit allowing service until 2 a.m. instead of the midnight default
Brazil's 2017 national law on fire prevention in places of public assembly, passed after the Kiss nightclub fire, signed with 12 vetoes.
A campaign launched in 2020 by filmmakers Erica Rose and Elina Street to count and support lesbian bars in the US.
a halt on new late-night licences in a defined area, as in inner Melbourne since 2008 for trading past 1 a.m.
the England and Wales law, in force Nov. 24, 2005, that replaced fixed pub hours with premises-by-premises licences set by councils

term: Licensing Board for the City of Boston
definition: The three-member board that grants, transfers and disciplines alcohol licenses in Boston; governor-appointed from 1906, mayor-appointed since the 2014 law.
the four tests under the Licensing Act 2003: crime and disorder, public safety, public nuisance and protecting children from harm; Scotland adds public health
Insurance covering claims that arise from serving alcohol.

aka: London Living Wage, Real Living Wage
definition: A voluntary UK pay benchmark based on living costs, used to measure low pay among night workers.
a state ceiling on hours with cities, counties or licensing boards setting actual hours inside it
a rule that bars new customers from entering after a set time while people already inside can stay until closing, as in Sydney from 2014 to 2021
Private, invitation-style dance party after David Mancuso's Loft, which began February 14, 1970, in New York.
An exit sign mounted near the floor, below smoke; required by Rhode Island's 2003 law in clubs of 150 or more.
The whole path out of a building - corridor, door, stairs - to the outside.
A club open to members rather than the general public; the Paradise Garage used this model and served no alcohol, so it could run past bar hours.
The amount a table or private party must spend on food and drink; if it is missed, the party pays the difference.

aka: Mayor's Office of Consumer Affairs and Licensing
definition: The Boston office whose Entertainment Licensing unit issues entertainment licenses, separate from the alcohol Licensing Board.
Spiking by injection rather than in a drink; UK police recorded 957 reports from May 2022 to April 2023.
The National Fire Protection Association's model code for life safety in buildings; it binds only where a state or city adopts it. Its 2006 edition made nightclub sprinkler rules permanent.
The standard for installing sprinkler systems. An NFPA 13 system controlled the fire in NIST's Station mock-up.
NFPA's model building code; its 2006 edition carried the same nightclub sprinkler rules as NFPA 101.
Berlin's smoking law, in force January 1, 2008, banning smoking in pubs, discotheques and clubs except in enclosed designated rooms.
A city post or office that represents the after-dark economy inside government, such as New York's Office of Nightlife.
London Underground's all-night Friday and Saturday service on selected lines, launched 19 August 2016.
All economic activity in a set night window, often 6 p.m. to 6 a.m., as defined by New York and London studies.
London's planned independent body for nightlife, recommended by the 2026 taskforce and launching later in 2026.
A club rule banning photography and filming on the dancefloor, usually enforced by a warning first and ejection for repeat offenders.
Flexible foam without fire retardant, used as acoustic lining; it ignited within 10 seconds of a pyrotechnic in NIST tests.
A license that cannot be sold and goes back to the Licensing Board when the business no longer needs it; free from the city under the 2024 law.
UK trade body for nightclubs and late-night businesses.
The most people a space is legally allowed to hold, based on floor area and exits; the number on the capacity placard.
The Victorian-era UK statute whose relevant parts the new harmful-substance offence replaces.
New York City office created in September 2017, run by a night mayor, with a 12-member advisory board.
Boston's city office for nighttime economy programs, set up in spring 2023 and led by Director Corean Reynolds.
An exit door that opens in the direction of travel so a pressing crowd can push it open; required after the Cocoanut Grove fire.
Passing an ID, stamp or wristband back to someone outside so a second person can use it to get in; some ID-scanner systems sell "anti-passback" alerts that flag the same ID scanned twice.
A deal where acts buy tickets upfront and must resell them.
A Boston permit required for a space holding 49 or more people, alongside an entertainment license.
The post-Prohibition system, created in 1933, that sets how many alcohol licenses a Massachusetts city or town may issue based on census population.
The cost of the liquor in a drink as a percentage of its menu price; vendor guidance (2025) puts liquor at roughly 15-20%.
the single licence under the Licensing Act 2003 that sets a venue's permitted hours and activities
A stated reason, such as a dress code or 'we're full', used to hide a discriminatory one.
The US national ban on alcohol, in effect January 17, 1920, to December 5, 1933.
A business open to the public, such as a nightclub, covered by anti-discrimination law.
A fully closed-off, designated room inside a Berlin venue where smoking is legally allowed.
US federal law whose provisions can make event organizers and venue owners liable for drug use at their events, as reported.
An ink mark or wristband showing a patron already paid and was checked, so they can return.
Massachusetts protection for a licensee who reasonably relied on an ID that turned out to be fake.
The UK Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994's definition of music at outdoor night-time gatherings police can act against.
After the Cocoanut Grove, revolving doors must fold flat or be flanked by conventional swinging doors, depending on occupant load.
Contract add-on listing an artist's technical and hospitality requirements.
A pre-Prohibition American bar, largely men-only, that the temperance movement targeted by name.
The 1988 UK club boom that followed London DJs' 1987 trip to Ibiza.
A Massachusetts license to sell alcohol for drinking on the premises, under MGL Chapter 138, Section 12; no sales 2 a.m. to 8 a.m.
Massachusetts legal term for any day other than Sunday, used in the 2 a.m. closing rule
At curated clubs, the door staff member who decides who enters, separate from security.
UK licence required for door supervisors under the Private Security Industry Act 2001; £190 and valid three years as listed in 2026.
A dance event with no alcohol served, such as the 'sugar free' Sunday edition of a Berlin party reported in 2025.
A designated area where people can carry open drinks bought from participating businesses; Boston piloted one at Temple Place in 2023 and 2024.
Dance events held earlier in the day or evening, often with little or no alcohol.
A parked bus used as an outreach and welfare point in a nightlife district.
An illegal bar during Prohibition; unlike the saloon, it drew men and women alike.
German for closing hour, a curfew on bars and restaurants; West Berlin abolished it in June 1949
Giving someone alcohol or drugs without their knowledge, in a drink or by needle.
Letting venues close at different times so crowds do not all reach the street at once; the aim of England and Wales's 2005 reform.
The US national monument designated June 24, 2016 by Proclamation 9465, marking the 1969 Stonewall Inn raid and riot.
Volunteers who patrol nightlife areas on high-risk nights in the UK.
Informal name for the large, branded, licensed 1990s clubs, such as Ministry of Sound and Cream, that grew into labels and festivals.
US federal venue aid program created in December 2020; $14.57 billion awarded by July 2022.
A specific Massachusetts license category, not a casual word for a bar; taverns must close from 1 a.m. to 8 a.m.
Electronic dance music developed in 1980s Detroit; the name was popularized by a 1988 UK compilation.
The campaign to reduce, then ban, alcohol consumption; in the US it grew from 1870s women's protests outside saloons.
An emergency change NFPA makes to a code between editions; NFPA used TIAs in July 2003 to require nightclub sprinklers and crowd managers.
UK nonprofit that opened the first Home Office-licensed regular drug checking service, in Bristol, in January 2024.

aka: Civil Rights Act of 1964, Title II
definition: US federal law barring race, color, religion and national-origin discrimination in covered places of entertainment; injunctions only, no damages.
An alcohol license the holder can sell to another business; scarce in Boston and reported in 2025 to resell for up to about $600,000.
A dance style that developed in Harlem ballrooms.
Competing at a ball in a themed category whose rules are set by the promoter.
Informal term for a deal where a promoter or artist leaves with an agreed share of the night's take; no trade definition verified.
The first DJ set of the night, meant to build the room gradually in tempo and volume without peaking it before later acts.
A staff member placed in a venue or nightlife district to look after people who are drunk, lost or vulnerable.
A license limited to beer and wine; under the 2024 Boston law holders may trade up to a non-transferable all-alcohol license.
A London pledge for venues and businesses on women's safety at night, with more than 650 signatories as of 2022.
